t: Jains hold that Mahavira, born a prince, abandoned royal life at about thirty, practised severe asceticism for twelve and a half years, attained Kevala Jnana, and then preached for thirty years.
He taught five vows, non-violence first among them, and a doctrine of many-sided reality, and Jains hold that his chief disciple Gautama Swami compiled his teachings as the Agamas.
Scholars agree that he lived, but they disagree about his dates, and they see him as a reformer of an older Jain or proto-Jain community led by Parshvanatha, not as its founder.
dyk: In 1974, for the 2,500th anniversary of Mahavira's nirvana, the mendicants of the Śvētāmbara, Digambara and Sthānakavāsī sects for the first time assembled on one platform and agreed on a common flag and emblem.
ev: Traditional date of Mahavira's birth at Kundagrama, as both Jain sects hold
He abandons royal life and becomes a naked ascetic, according to the Ācārāṅga Sūtra
After twelve and a half years
He attains Kevala Jnana under a Sāla tree on the bank of the Rijuvalika River
He initiates his first disciples, the eleven Ganadharas, led by Indrabhuti Gautama
Śvētāmbara date of his nirvana at Pawapuri; the Digambaras say 510 BCE
The earliest known images of him are made at Mathura
The Akota hoard's bronze of Mahavira as Jivantasvami, the earliest known clothed Jain idol, is dated
Jain sects hold a joint commemoration of the 2,500th anniversary of his nirvana

f.born: Traditionally in 599 BCE at Kundagrama in the Kingdom of the Videhas, in present-day Bihar, to King Siddhartha of the Nāya tribe and Queen Trishala
f.died: Traditionally at Pawapuri in Bihar, in 527 BCE according to the Śvetāmbaras and 510 BCE according to the Digambaras; some scholars date his death much later
f.role: Held by Jains to be the 24th and final Tirthankara of the present time cycle; described by historians as a reformer of an existing Jain community, the Niganthas
f.known: Teaching the five vows; ahimsa as the supreme virtue; the soul and karma; anekantavada; twelve and a half years of asceticism; the four-fold order of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen
